Positions.Branch/Division: Planning, Evaluation and Resource Management Div

Responsibility: Full latitude to analyze and elaborate on existing management information; to assess the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of programs, operations and initiatives; to monitor and assess management accountability for departmental programs; and to develop/recommend ways to improve departmental policies, programs and operations. This latitude extends to the assessment of strategic and operational responsibilities; legislation, regulations and compliance; program, policy and initiative design; the effectiveness of strategies, policies, and program delivery mechanisms; organizational structure; the socio-economic impacts; the achievement of program, policy and initiative objectives; risk assessment; change management strategies; and resource allocation and budgeting.

Full latitude to analyze and assess Central Agency government-wide policies as well as departmental policies/programs and, by developing and recommending alternatives, cause these Central Agencies to make well-informed and sound decisions on changes to their legislation, policy, regulations, programs, and/or operations. This information also contributes to effective governance and improved accountability through its impact on departmental and Central Agency business lines. It is used by departmental Senior Management to make studied decisions respecting organizational performance and changes to the structure, management and delivery of their programs and services; action on legislative, regulatory and policy changes; alternate means to respond to emerging client demands; strengthening strategic and business planning; and the effective allocation of resources.

There is full latitude to scope, plan, authorize, and guide the collection and analysis of the foundation data in order to create new information about programs and their effectiveness, to decide what data, from which sources will be used, and how information will be created, developed or gathered. While general research, and evaluation principles and standards are followed, the incumbent has the latitude to innovate by pushing the boundaries of existing methods, interpreting the findings, and determining materiality in order to craft the reporting of results. The information provides Senior Management with independent, new and unique insights into the subject programs/topics and is used to make informed decisions concerning the scope, structure, redefinition or termination of major programs, initiatives, operations or activities. The information provides assurance on the level of performance of the specified program(s), new interpretations of program standards/performance, and to make executive decisions intra-departmentally or interdepartmentally.

Provide direction/expertise, and adapt concepts to develop and originate methodologies, tools and techniques to support the evolution of and use of professional practices and government-wide standards for the conduct of evaluation and review activities. This information is shared with colleagues, Senior Management, Central Agencies, OGDs, and other professional and governmental organizations.

From an analysis of the potential impact of wider departmental-governmental management issues on the scope, objectives, prioritization and resourcing of the evaluation program, prioritize proposed projects for the annual departmental Evaluation Plan, and provide input on issues and strategic considerations for use by the departmental Review Committee and Branch management in short and long term strategic planning.

In addition to evaluation-review reports as described above, develop oral and written presentations, briefing materials, position papers, Parliamentary questions and answers, and other documents to communicate salient issues and expert opinions. This information is used by Senior Management and by stakeholders to fully understand evaluation-review issues, results and recommendations, to implement corrective action, and to make related decisions pertaining to the management and delivery of policies, programs, initiatives, and services.

Develop, create and communicate information to Senior Management and to stakeholders in the form of assurances, evaluations advice, and recommendations pertaining to departmental programs, policies and initiatives.

The work requires ongoing consultations and discussions with senior management throughout the Department in order to develop and maintain a current and comprehensive understanding of business functions, goals and objectives and to define the services that are, and will be, required and expected from the Corporate Planning function.
The work requires integration of strategic plans with those of other Branches and Fields of the Department requiring ongoing consultation with representatives of other planning organizations.

The work requires interaction with senior management staff in the headquarters and regional offices to develop and promote acceptance of a common program evaluation and strategic planning methodology. The role also requires the development, monitoring and the implementation of policies, procedures, practices and standards for program evaluation.
Interaction with program staff, working in a complex matrix management environment is required to ensure that policies, standards and practices are reflective of current government trends.

Activities, recommendations and decisions concerning the feasibility and establishment of long range strategies and plans and the development of policies, standards and procedures will significantly influence Agency operations and resource allocations over the short and long term and provide the Department with a viable long term strategy to maximize efficient resource utilization.

Recommendations are made to the Director, as a result of performance measurement and operational reviews to effect changes in Divisional plans and programs to better meet client needs and expectations and ensure that the Division is meeting its goals and objectives.

Decisions are made, in consultation with colleagues (planning analysts) regarding the development, use and maintenance of various system applications such as the Corporate Strategic Planning system which will significantly influence all aspects of systems development, implementation, maintenance and use.

The work involves continuing study of emerging issues, trends and developments impacting government operations (i.e., strategic planning processes, performance evaluations, program evaluations and program review ) in order to develop and recommend strategies, plans, policies and procedures that will position the Branch and the Department to meet the program evaluation and program delivery challenges of the future.

Judgement is required to assess the long term benefits of introducing new governance policies and planning methodologies to the work environment which requires a sound knowledge of Government trends and directions. The Planning Analyst is responsible for reviewing proposals put forth by senior managers, assessing the feasibility of proposals from an efficiency and effectiveness perspective and recommending approval of plans or alternate resourcing based on availability of funding (envelope or corporate funding).

The work involves establishing performance measurement criteria and processes; monitoring, evaluating and assessing results and recommending modification of operations, procedures and practices to ensure adherence to approved levels of quality and service.

The work involves developing a planning framework/process that will ensure identification, prioritization and integration of the needs of clients; ensure linkages to relevant Central Agency priorities and initiatives; and take into account other information-related initiatives of the Corporate Services Sector.

The work involves monitoring Central Agency policies, analyzing the impact of same on the Department and preparing briefings, policy and position papers and submissions on behalf of senior management.
No specific requirement.

Manage multi-disciplinary human resources assigned to individual projects in a matrix, including subject-matter experts, colleagues, seconded staff, employees of other government departments and agencies, professional consultants, and/or students.

Simultaneously lead a series of evaluation project teams composed of departmental specialists, technical experts, statisticians, analysts, evaluators, and/or students. Specific team leadership responsibilities include: develop broad priorities and work plans; authorize resource levels; establish operational guidelines, standards and methodologies; organize, coordinate, and assign work; set work schedules and short-term plans; allocate people across the teams, such that skills and numbers are appropriate to the work load and evaluation issues; facilitate the project team's identification of mutual roles, goals and responsibilities; provide on-the-job technical guidance, and coaching; provide learning opportunities to develop skills and abilities; monitor and evaluate work performance against planned deliverables; resolve and reconcile assignments across teams as the work progresses.

Plans, initiates, co-ordinates, and provides expert advice and guidance for multi-disciplinary project work or teams in support of the development of results-based approaches. Organizes the work of departmental groups, to achieve multiple objectives on a regular basis. Chairs, facilitates or participates in meetings, committees, and working groups and organizes, plans and co-ordinates the work of the people involved on results-based issues.
Plans, initiates and develops alternative ways to accomplish objectives, including partnerships and projects with other divisions, branches, and Fields. This responsibility is shared.

Provide leadership and mentorship by establishing objectives for new staff, assigning responsibilities, establishing work procedures, directing work, providing technical and operational guidance, and assessing and evaluating performance.

Chair and or facilitate departmental, interdepartmental, or professional meetings, committees, workshops, focus groups and working groups which involve evaluation staff, contract resources and representatives of departmental organizations, both senior managers and working level employees. These responsibilities are sometimes shared.

Initiate and lead consultative processes to promote cooperation and sharing of information among members of the evaluation community and professional organizations. These responsibilities are shared. Demonstrate adherence to ethical principles, corporate values, professional standards, and applicable codes of conduct, and promote trust, confidence and integrity.
A. PLANNING AND CONTROLLING:
Initiates, reviews, and prepares cost-analyses, proposals and recommendations for the use of funds.

Initiates, devises and recommends more effective ways of doing the work that contribute to more effective use of funds and other resources. This activity is performed in accordance with Finance and Administration Act guidelines and established practices.

Participates in financial planning and reporting for the division and develops and defends recommendations to senior officials regarding the establishment and modification of division budgets and financial plans. The incumbent has the authority to develop and explain proposals and recommendations; the authority to allocate funds, however, rests with the Director.
B. ACQUIRING FUNDS:
No specific requirement
C. SPENDING FUNDS:

Develops terms of reference for consultant studies, prepares evaluation criteria, and recommends the award of contracts by choosing the best option as they relate to value and cost. Receives invoices from consultants and authorizes the payment of the invoices at the agreed upon price upon satisfactory completion of the work by the contractor with latitude within departmental guidelines, the FAA, government contracting regulations and financial policies.

Negotiates contracts for specific projects/studies with external organizations (consultants) and monitors financial accounting procedures to ensure that spending is cost-effective and properly accounted for. This activity is performed in accordance with established practices and guidelines.

Initiates, reviews and authorises the purchase of publications, information, data and various office supplies including computer hardware and software in accordance with Treasury Board guidelines and in consultation with the Director.

Use government credit cards, traveller’s cheques and taxi chits to purchase services in accordance with the employer approved Authorization to Travel and the provisions of departmental policy and the TBS Travel Directive.

Ensure custody of, and protect confidential, secret and top-secret documents as well as proprietary and commercially confidential documents. This information is used to undertake evaluations and reviews. Often these documents are highly sensitive and cannot be copied. These documents usually cannot be replaced without substantial effort.

Create, maintain and has custody of active hard copy and electronic project working files and Senior Management performance reviews and evaluations. These contain evidence (specimens, analysis-documentation, project findings, conclusions and recommendations) gathered during the course of evaluations and reviews. In many instances they are the Department’s only official record and depository of project results. Project team members use the working paper files to perform their work in delivering the evaluation-review services to departmental Senior Management and stakeholders. If lost, some documentation could be replicated or reconstructed from other sources, while other documentation would extremely be difficult to replace.

Plays a leading role in the completion and review of the departmental Planning Reporting and Accountability Structures, Business Plans, Reports on Plans and Priorities, Departmental Performance Reports to ensure ongoing improvements have been implemented, and where appropriate, compliance with government standards, guidelines and practices. These documents are part of the Estimates submitted to Parliament. There may be a requirement to negotiate corrective action with the client department or agency to comply with the guidelines and practices. The incumbent has moderate latitude in choosing appropriate corrective action. Liaises with the Industry Portfolio Office and the Treasury Board Secretariat on an ongoing basis, to ensure compliance to established standards.

Monitors and performs quality control over work performed under contract to ensure that private sector consultants comply with the terms and conditions of contracts. Decisions are taken under the applicable sections of the Financial Administration Act and the Treasury Board Contracting Regulations. Has authority to direct work be redone or brought up to contract specifications and quality requirements and can re-negotiate or recommend contract termination. Failure to comply could result in the cancellation of the contract, refusal to pay for work done or partial payment for work done. This responsibility is not shared.
Skills: The work requires experienced use and application of the following research and assessment concepts/methods: advanced statistical methods and techniques in such areas as program model design and interpretation, forecasting, and cost-benefit and cost/effectiveness analyses, including social cost-benefit analysis; problem analysis, hypothesis formulation and validation; quantitative approaches including statistical sampling and projection, regression, and correlation, present value and sensitivity analyses; benchmarking; ratio and trend analysis; survey/questionnaire design and use; simulation; options analysis; performance measurement; interviewing techniques; focus groups; and the design and integration of sophisticated computer-based and manual evaluation methodologies.

Expert-level Program Evaluation knowledge is needed to design new statistical research tools which support the production of concrete alternatives and options in making recommendations to achieve more focused program delivery; to develop new techniques for attribution and representation of the relationships between program goals, operations and results on social and economic levels, adding to the generally available methods and frameworks for Program Evaluation in the community; to select and direct the application by project team members of the appropriate concepts, methods and techniques to complex evaluation frameworks, evaluation assessments and evaluation studies or reviews; and, as the authoritative source of expertise on formulating evaluation methodologies and interpreting results, to be functional advisor to staff engaged in evaluation projects where the staff's primary background may not be Program Evaluation. This extensive knowledge is also required in order to act as the department expert and focal point to Senior Management and Treasury Board on all aspects of Program Evaluation in the Department.

Knowledge is required of computer software applications to conduct analysis and document project results, including specialized software such as statistical sampling, computer assisted techniques, automated working papers, and flowcharting.

Knowledge of theories, principle and techniques of performance accountability management, which includes results-based management, performance frameworks, third party and alternative delivery accountability trends, planning, reporting and accountability structures, performance indicators, and review, auditing and evaluation methods and techniques. This knowledge is required to manage and provide direction to client departments regarding modifications and improvements to specific reporting mechanisms and frameworks. This knowledge is also required to lead and provide guidance to project teams and working groups.

Knowledge of social science research methods, techniques and practices, including multi-disciplinary analysis methods, to carry out analysis on a variety of approaches regarding performance and accountability framework in other levels of government, other jurisdictions and in the private sector. This knowledge is used to provide advice and guidance to improve the departmental capacity for quality performance reporting to Parliament and the public.

Knowledge of planning methods, techniques and practices, including those associated with time-management, strategic planning and financial analysis. This knowledge is required to lead and provide direction to project teams and working groups regarding the development and modification of division budgets, financial plans, strategic goals and policy initiatives.

Knowledge of program management methods, techniques and practices, which includes public administration and project management. This knowledge is required to manage and provide direction to project and consultation initiatives. This knowledge is also required to establish and determine project priorities, objectives and goals and to develop project plans.

Knowledge is required of theories and principles of Project Management, organizational leadership and behaviour, management of change, group dynamics, and existing or emerging public sector and private sector human resource management themes and issues to direct, organize and coordinate multi-disciplinary project teams, and to provide advice, opinions and recommendations to Senior Management. Knowledge is required of theories, concepts and techniques of business and public administration, including contract management and quality assurance, in order to effectively manage a portfolio of program evaluation, and review projects.

Knowledge is required of marketing, negotiation and communications principles, methods, tools and techniques to develop clear, concise and effective reports, executive summaries, briefing notes and presentations to inform Senior Management as well as to conduct effective interviews and facilities focus groups.

Knowledge is required of computer software applications to conduct analysis and document project results, including specialized software such as statistical sampling, computer assisted techniques, automated working papers and flowcharting.

Skill in synthesising information from diverse disciplines (environmental science, economics, and public policy administration, etc.) to facilitate the development and the implementation of interdepartmental performance frameworks.

Knowledge of theories, principles and techniques of consultation, management, conflict resolution, small group process, interviewing and counselling to be able to manage, influence employees, colleagues and others, to lead project teams, negotiate contracts for services, and negotiate agreements with other institutions.
Knowledge of tools and techniques for preparing and delivering oral and visual presentations to inform, persuade or influence a variety of audiences of the benefits of a particular course of action.
The work requires:
A. OWN WORK UNIT:

Knowledge is required of the organization and objectives of the evaluation division; the strategic direction, culture, structure and organization, mandate, objectives, policies, procedures and work tools of the Field, branch, division; and the structure and organization of project work teams, their mandates and objectives. This knowledge is required to set and achieve operational objectives, assess compliance, achieve results in an effective and efficient manner, and develop new or improved business services, policies, systems and procedures.
Knowledge of the policies, procedures, guidelines, mandate and personnel of the Branch:
B. OWN DEPARTMENT OR AGENCY:
Knowledge of the policies, procedures, guidelines, mandate and personnel of the department:

The knowledge is required to identify issues, develop evaluation projects, to eliminate duplication of effort in planning for and carrying out program evaluations, to provide assurance and recommendations to departmental performance and decision making, and to recommend changes to legislation, policies, program structure, organization structure, and program delivery mechanisms.
C. OTHER FEDERAL DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES:
Knowledge of the personnel, organization, priorities, policies, mandate, objectives, goals and programs of a wide range of client departments and organizations:

Knowledge is required of the Parliamentary system and machinery of government, and its expectations for the Department, policy making and legislative processes, government priorities, and current and emerging management issues; the mandate, policies, programs, operations and reporting processes of Parliamentary committees, central agencies, and other federal government departments; and the role of Treasury Board and the privy Council Office.
D. CANADIAN PRIVATE SECTOR AND OTHER PUBLIC SECTORS:

Knowledge of personnel and organisation of different orders of government (provincial, territorial, municipal), the academic community, and non-government organisations in order to effectively communicate on performance and accountability approaches, methods, theories, studies, and analysis for the purpose of strengthening performance reporting to Parliament and the public.

Knowledge of think tanks that are working in the area of citizen engagement, societal indicators and quality of life modelling, to carry out analysis regarding alternative performance and accountability frameworks and approaches (e.g. National Statistical Council).
E. INTERNATIONAL PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTOR:

Knowledge of personnel and organisation of different national governments, international organisations (International Statistical Agencies), the international academic community, and non-government organisations in order to effectively communicate on performance and accountability approaches, methods, theories, studies, and analysis for the purpose of strengthening performance reporting to Parliament and the public.
F. LEGISLATION AND REGULATIONS:

The incumbent requires knowledge of certain sections of legislation related to client departments and to STC reporting and reviews regulations and requirements. This knowledge is required to: a) monitor and track the fulfilment of key reporting requirements and obligations by client departments and organizations; b) provide advice on appropriate courses of action for client departments and organizations regarding the development of reporting and performance review mechanisms and frameworks; and c) to handle and process sensitive information and documentation related to client departments and reporting processes.
Knowledge of government travel directives/regulations to ensure own compliance with same.
A. COMMUNICATION IN:
The work requires:

Listening and evaluation skills to interpret verbal and non-verbal communication when receiving information and feedback from colleagues, managers and departments to understand the meaning behind the questions, to determine what their concerns are, to retain salient points and synthesize information on a variety of issues of differing complexity, to understand opinion and points of view, and to gauge underlying intentions. These skills are necessary both to adjust the techniques used in exchanging information and to define products and services in response to a better appreciation of clients' and managers' needs.

Listening skills to understand the needs and concerns of employees in the Unit, in order to solve research problems and expedite the completion of the work. Listening skills are also needed to interpret verbal and non-verbal communication of members of multi-disciplinary teams, involving representative from other departments. These individuals often have widely differing policy views and positions on specific issues and conflicting ideas on how to conduct policy processes. Tact and diplomacy are required to avoid or resolve conflict.

Reading and listening skills, to maintain knowledge of key developments, research and innovations related to reporting and accountability processes and techniques, to attend conferences and meetings of professional associations related to auditing, financial analysis, and accountability reporting, to analyse and assess a wide range of alternative accountability approaches, strategies and processes, to liase and consult with academics, researchers and related specialists regarding a wide range of issues and innovations. These skills are required to address policy issues, to assist in designing and developing new and innovative methodological approaches which improve analysis, and to remain current on development within the sector to be able to advise colleagues, managers and departments about various issues and analytical approaches.
B. COMMUNICATION OUT:
The work requires:

Speaking and writing skills are required in much of the work. Instances include: negotiating with and obtaining approval of Senior Management and program managers concerning the nature, themes, timelines and resources of evaluations to be undertaken; negotiating with consultants and later resolving differences over project terms of reference, contract deliverables and payment; directing multi-disciplinary project teams, mediating and resolving conflicts with/among clients and staff on politically sensitive and/or complex projects; convince parties to take action; consulting with program managers and Senior Management; preparing non-project documents, such as plans, reports, briefings, and presentation material for the Senior Management. The subject matter often involves politically sensitive or contentious government-wide program/policy issues requiring persuasive arguments to gain acceptance and commitment.

Skill is required to write balanced and convincing evaluation reports. There is a requirement to convince Senior Management to change their positions and/or observed corporate behaviours and to accept what is being recommended. The circumstances of the briefing and presentations can be adversarial and managers are often hostile and resistant. At times, it is necessary to explain and extensively reinforce the message, repeatedly and in multiple ways, with the ultimate aim of persuading highly resistant Departmental and/or Central Agency senior managers and decision-makers to change their views, to adopt additional or different approaches and controls, to change the structure of a subject program and its activities significantly, or even to cancel a program.

Oral and written skills, to make presentations to large audiences, consult with officials from client departments and organizations, to clarify and explain key guidelines, priorities, objectives and strategic goals related to the reporting and review of program evaluation and performance. The incumbent must have the writing skills to develop and revise complex frameworks, methodologies, and systems, and to develop and explain proposals for client officials regarding the development of approaches and strategies. These tasks are made more difficult by having to present information to audiences/departments with widely differing backgrounds and expertise in the subject matter.

Verbal and writing skills, to provide leadership and direction to client consultation working groups and project teams, to establish and implement key project priorities, objectives, guidelines and strategic goals, and to develop, clarify and explain project plans. The incumbent must have the writing and verbal skills required to present and defend positions/recommendations to project members, and to develop, revise and present key project and team proposals and recommendations to senior officials and officials from client departments regarding the development and modification of reporting frameworks and strategies.

Assertive oral and written communication skills to be able to effectively implement conflict resolution, and negotiation strategies in meetings with colleagues, managers and departments, and to be able to achieve understanding, consensus or compromise among groups of individuals with different perspectives and interests to take, consider or support specific actions. Skill is required to write balanced and convincing evaluation reports. There is a requirement to convince Senior Management to change their positions and or observed corporate behaviours and to accept what is being recommended.

Speaking and writing skills are also required to act as an effective departmental representative on various interdepartmental committees with individuals from a variety of disciplines and knowledge levels, including senior officials and colleagues from central agencies, professional associations and external organizations.

Writing presentations and public speaking are needed to articulate policy approaches and strategies, to brief departmental management on recurring policy issues and key project problems and delays, and to develop and explain recommendations and proposals regarding the modification of strategic goals, objectives, policies and initiatives. The information being communicated is frequently complex, covering cross-sectoral linkages that are not widely understood. The subject matter is frequently controversial, or conflicts with the policy views and positions of target audiences, requiring careful choice of words and the ability to anticipate and deflect critical responses. The incumbent must also have the skills to respond to complex, challenging questions and at times to present aggregate information to Members of Parliament and/or to brief the Deputy Minister of STC.

Dexterity and co-ordination skills are required on a daily basis to operate a computer keyboard and mouse to search, retrieve, and manipulate and transform information and data from information bases, the Internet and Intranet as well as to type briefing notes, memoranda, notes, reports, and analytical documents. Any requirement for proficiency, precision and speed in the conduct of this activity is under the control of the incumbent.
Effort: Strategic thinking is required to evaluate the relevance, success and cost-effectiveness of programs, policies, and initiatives, while considering the departmental mandate and vision, broad government priorities and objectives, and the social and economic goals intended to be achieved. Effort is required to research, identify, analyze and often reconcile complex, multi-dimensional, interrelated variables and issues; assess the range of socio-economic and/or environmental impacts; and produce authoritative options and strategic advice based on conclusions which are strategically focused, objective, evidence-based, timely, pertinent and credible. The work entails adapting econometric analyses using advanced statistical methodologies, and contributing to processes, tools and techniques (e.g. RPPs and DPRs). There is a requirement to provide Senior Management with expert advice in the design and development phase of new programs, policies, and initiatives; the integration of evaluation methodologies; the development of strategic, annual and long-term evaluation plans; resource allocation; priority setting; strategic planning; policy development; performance measurement; and monitoring and reporting.

As the evaluation expert, ensure methodologies are properly applied and provide technical expertise to the most difficult project demands for research tools and approaches. Intellectual effort is needed to apply alternative approaches and solutions to identified problems, to design frameworks (e.g. accountability and performance measurement) for the analysis of diverse qualitative and quantitative information, and to develop new tools for statistical analysis in response to unique problems. In formulating an approach, various factors must be considered including government initiatives/priorities, technological evolution, culture and interpersonal dynamics within the client's organization, policy requirements, and competing factors based on diverse interests.

Intellectual effort is required to create models of the review area to build an understanding of it; judge the evidence gathered in relation to the review criteria; identify linkages, causes and effects relating to the preliminary finding; judge each finding in terms of materiality, sensitivity and risk; develop conclusions; and make recommendations. The areas under evaluation are highly sensitive and require solid proof of findings. Views of stakeholders with differing or conflicting views must be integrated into the analyses, adding to the level of effort required. Additional constraints that hamper the analysis include information gaps that require the development and use of proxy measures. Effort is required to ensure a quality control and to challenge assumptions and underlying logic used by multi-disciplinary teams to develop conclusions and recommendations intended to resolve issues and secure acceptance. Difficulties arise from the need to ensure that recommendations are linked to departmental strategic priorities, objectives and the needs of Senior Management.

Intellectual effort is required to formulate departmental problems and needs objectively and accurately, and to compile, analyze and synthesize a wide range of information. Typically, there are many, often conflicting elements - political concerns, Central Agency interests, interdepartmental relationships, environmental and other factors - that have to be taken into consideration. In some cases, it is necessary to develop new conceptual frameworks in order to understand the issues and their relationships. There is often very little time to capture the essence of the problem and to arrive at a formulation; Senior Management and/or program managers may urge the adoption of a particular interpretation of the problem, or conversely, strive to avoid having a problem defined; data is frequently incomplete and may be misleading.

Effort is required to evaluate policy, program and regulatory issues with respect to their implications for the implementation of results-based management, improved reporting to Parliament, and to provide easier access to performance and collective results policy objectives. Effort is also required to evaluate these issues vertically with respect to their impact on departments and Parliament. Effort is required to develop innovative and original tools and approaches to address the increasingly horizontal and vertical aspects of policy, program delivery and regulatory initiatives. Traditional approaches and tools are often too narrow in focus to address the complexities required in such reviews and analysis. The application of accountability and results-based management theories and techniques to the analysis of vertical and horizontal interactions represents often a leading edge research. The outcome can be made difficult by the limited availability of resources, information, data, the need for timely response, and competing and rapidly changing priorities.

Intellectual effort is required to conceptualize, develop and carry out analytical reviews, which entails developing strategic recommendations and proposals, and writing reports, working papers, background and briefing material for the direct use of analysts and senior officials in the directorate. Effort is required to understand the context and application of the required analysis and information and to provide functional direction and advise to analysts in choosing from among a variety of information and data sources, analytical techniques and tools those which are most appropriate for the application in question given the short imposed time frames.

Effort is required to review, conceptualize, and write, in easily understood and persuasive language, reports, correspondence, background and briefing material, based on the results of analysis of complex issues, and on information drawn from a wide variety of sources with varying degrees of technical complexity, for the use of audiences, both internal and external, with widely differing backgrounds and technical understanding of the subject matter or the ability to understand and use this information in their work. This effort can be challenging due to the lack of data and information or lack of existing tools or frameworks of analysis, which address the multiple objectives that departments and the government have in terms of accountability and reporting to Parliament.

Effort is required to identify, describe, review and revise key messages for government-wide or targeted communications initiatives which contribute to the understanding and resolution of policy, program or regulatory issues on the capacity of departments to manage for results, and to identify and utilize the most effective means of communicating these messages to various internal and external target audiences which have varying degrees of technical or policy understanding. Such requirements occur on a regular basis with multi-departmental, internal working groups and project teams, often under tight time frames, with the added difficulty of having to adjust to concurrently evolving departmental interests and priorities and government policy directions.

Effort is required to develop and maintain a practical and conceptual understanding of advances nationally and in other countries with respect to accountability and results-based management theory, and the tools and techniques of analysis in these areas. Effort is required to integrate these advances in theory, tools, and techniques into the work of the section. The changing nature and learning environment of these advances and the need for innovation and originality in the development and design of approaches and techniques poses an ongoing intellectual challenge.

Effort is required to anticipate departments and the government requirements, and to proactively design, develop and distribute hard copy and electronic information products which meet these requirements and minimizes the section resources needed to serve these emerging client needs. Evolving client needs, capabilities of information and data sources, information management and presentation technology, and analytical techniques and methods increase the intellectual effort needed to effectively carry out this function.

Attention is required to analyse complex issues and interpret and understand them in order to develop policy-focused papers, briefings and recommendations. This requirement accounts for 25 to 30% of the total working time, averaged over one year.

Chairing, participating or facilitating meetings with colleagues, senior management, or officials from other departments over periods of one to three hours requires sustained auditory and visual attention to focus in order to understand policy discussions, to be able to make effective contributions, and to influence the direction and outcome of meetings. The inability to sustain focused attention may result in missing key information, misinterpretation of comments, the provision of incorrect or unintended messages, or loss of control over the meeting. Deterrents to sustained attention include participants speaking at the same time, and side conversations. This activity represents 20 to 25% of total work time, averaged over one year.

Psychological and emotional effort is required to maintain composure, professionalism and good working relationships when chairing or facilitating meetings of multi-stakeholders work team during which sensitive and contentious issues of Treasury Board Secretariat policy and/or guidelines are discussed. There is some control over the occurrence and frequency of such meetings, but little or no control over the reactions of individuals.

Psychological/emotional efforts are required on an ongoing basis to maintain professionalism when dealing with politically sensitive issues, adapting to shifting priorities and imposed short deadlines to meet the multiple, competing and sometimes conflicting demands of management and senior management. There is little or no control over the occurrence, frequency and duration of such situations.

Psychological/emotional efforts are required to maintain composure and professionalism when promoting or defending the position of Treasury Board Secretariat, which are not necessarily consistent with one's own views, particularly in situations which are contentious, where the actions/positions of the Secretariat are not welcomed, and where the audience is hostile. Such meetings occur several times annually. There is no control over how and when audiences choose to express their views.

Psychological and emotional effort is required to maintain composure and professionalism in working with teams, determining priorities, meeting tight project deadlines, negotiating and consulting with TBS and IPO and providing constructive feedback to processes and methodologies. There is limited control over the occurrence, frequency and duration of these situations.
Urgent high profile evaluations requested by the Minister, Deputy Minister, or Senior Managers can cause immediate changes to existing assignments and priorities.
